questions.prompt: A call with strike $100 and one year to expiry costs $10.45. The stock is $100, and the present value of $100 is $95.12. What must the put with the same strike and expiry cost?
questions.explanation: Put-call parity says call − put = stock − present value of strike = 100 − 95.12 = 4.88. So the put is 10.45 − 4.88 = $5.57.

questions.prompt: The put trades at $5.57 but the call is quoted at $11.45, $1.00 too high. Which set of trades locks in $1.00 today with no risk?
options: Buy the call, sell the put, sell a share, lend $95.12
Sell the call, buy the put, buy a share, borrow $95.12
Buy the call and the put, borrow $95.12
Sell the call and the put, lend $95.12
questions.explanation: Selling the overpriced call and buying the cheaper side gives 11.45 − 5.57 − 100 + 95.12 = $1.00 today. At expiry the share, put and sold call are worth $100, which repays the loan.

questions.prompt: Why must a call plus $95.12 of cash cost the same today as a put plus one share?
options: Because both pay the larger of the stock price and $100 at expiry, in every case
Because calls and puts always have the same premium
Because the stock price is equal to the strike
questions.explanation: Two baskets that pay the same in every outcome must cost the same. If they did not, an arbitrage would buy the cheap basket and sell the expensive one.
